summary: amortization period is what the Balloon payment calculator works out, and it gets there from the interest rate, the periods ballon, the periods and the extra monthly payment. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Balloon payment calculator work?
sections.html:
The Balloon payment calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports amortization period in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the compounding method and the payment frequency); then you type in the interest rate, the periods ballon, the periods and the extra monthly payment.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Balloon payment calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Amortization period=periods ÷ payment frequency
Balloon payment after=periods ballon ÷ payment frequency
Pmt calc=(interest rate, amortization period, M, payment frequency, loan amount, balloon payment after, extra monthly payment, 0)
Balance=(interest rate, amortization period, M, payment frequency, loan amount, balloon payment after, extra monthly payment, 2)
Total pmt=(interest rate, amortization period, M, payment frequency, loan amount, balloon payment after, extra monthly payment, 3)
Difference in balances=(interest rate, amortization period, M, payment frequency, loan amount, balloon payment after, extra monthly payment, 4)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Time, opening in years / months
  • Time, opening in years
  • %, opening in percent
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Balloon payment calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the interest rate, the periods ballon and the periods — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Balloon payment calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns amortization period, derived from the interest rate, the periods ballon and the periods. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Balloon payment calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the interest rate, the periods ballon, the periods and the extra monthly payment, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter loan amount in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Loan amount opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Balloon payment calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
